# ConceptARC DSL program (the verifier is this descriptor, run by the interpreter below):
# {"action": {"op": "remove_selected"},"selector": {"op": "central_object"}}
# Entry point: output = transform_dsl_program(program, input_grid)

# --- action: how the selection is turned into the output grid ---

def transform_dsl_program(program: DslProgram, grid: Grid) -> Grid:
    # Dispatch trimmed to the branch(es) this program uses.
    """Apply a default DSL program to an input grid.

    Args:
      program (DslProgram): DSL program.
      grid (Grid): Input grid.

    Returns:
      Grid: Output grid.
    """
    selection = select_scene_objects(program.selector, grid)
    action_op = program.action.get("op")
    if action_op == "remove_selected":
        return remove_object(grid, expect_object(selection))

# --- selection: which cells/objects the program operates on ---

def select_scene_objects(selector: dict[str, Any], grid: Grid) -> SceneSelection:
    # Dispatch trimmed to the branch(es) this program uses.
    """Select object(s) from a grid using a DSL selector expression.

    Args:
      selector (dict[str, Any]): Selector expression.
      grid (Grid): Input grid.

    Returns:
      SceneSelection: Selected object or object pair.
    """
    op = selector.get("op")
    if op == "central_object":
        return _central_object(
            objects,
            grid_center(grid),
            _excluded_objects(selector, grid),
            "central_object",
        )

# --- helpers the branches above reach (ConceptARC-GEN, verify side only; `common.grid(w, h, c)` is ARC-GEN's blank-grid constructor) ---

Grid = list[list[int]]

Pixel = tuple[int, int]

Bounds = tuple[int, int, int, int]

def bounds(pixels: Sequence[Pixel]) -> Bounds:
    """Return row/column bounds for pixels.

    Args:
      pixels (Sequence[Pixel]): Pixels to bound.

    Returns:
      Bounds: ``min_row, min_col, max_row, max_col``.
    """
    rows = [row for row, _ in pixels]
    cols = [col for _, col in pixels]
    return (min(rows), min(cols), max(rows), max(cols))

SceneSelection = Union[SceneCell, SceneCellGroup, SceneCellPatch, SceneCount, SceneRowRun, SceneObject, tuple[SceneObject, SceneObject], SceneObjectGroup, SceneObjectReferenceGroup, SceneShapeInstance, SceneShapeInstanceGroup]

def object_bounds(obj: SceneObject) -> tuple[int, int, int, int]:
    """Return object bounds.

    Args:
      obj (SceneObject): Object to inspect.

    Returns:
      tuple[int, int, int, int]: ``min_row, min_col, max_row, max_col``.
    """
    return bounds(obj.pixels)

def object_center(obj: SceneObject) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Return the bounding-box center for an object.

    This point is the DSL's object reference point for distance-based selectors
    such as ``nearest_object`` and ``central_object``. For sparse visual objects
    such as dotted outlines, it is the center of the whole visual bounding box,
    not the center of an individual dot. The returned point may be fractional;
    a 4-pixel horizontal line, for example, has a reference center between two
    cells rather than a center cell.

    Args:
      obj (SceneObject): Object to inspect.

    Returns:
      tuple[float, float]: Row and column center.
    """
    min_row, min_col, max_row, max_col = object_bounds(obj)
    return ((min_row + max_row) / 2, (min_col + max_col) / 2)

def grid_center(grid: Grid) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Return the geometric center of a grid.

    The returned point may be fractional for even-width or even-height grids.

    Args:
      grid (Grid): Grid to inspect.

    Returns:
      tuple[float, float]: Row and column center.
    """
    return ((len(grid) - 1) / 2, (len(grid[0]) - 1) / 2)

def _bbox_area(obj: SceneObject) -> int:
    """Return object bounding-box area.

    Args:
      obj (SceneObject): Object to inspect.

    Returns:
      int: Bounding-box area.
    """
    min_row, min_col, max_row, max_col = object_bounds(obj)
    return (max_row - min_row + 1) * (max_col - min_col + 1)

def _central_object(objects: list[SceneObject], anchor: tuple[float, float], excluded_objects: set[SceneObject], selector_name: str) -> SceneObject:
    """Return the object centered exactly on an anchor.

    Args:
      objects (list[SceneObject]): Candidate visual scene objects.
      anchor (tuple[float, float]): Required object-center point.
      excluded_objects (set[SceneObject]): Objects to skip.
      selector_name (str): Selector name used in error messages.

    Returns:
      SceneObject: Smallest object whose bounding-box center is exactly the
      anchor.
    """
    candidates = [obj for obj in objects if obj not in excluded_objects and object_center(obj) == anchor]
    if not candidates:
        raise ValueError(selector_name + ' selector found no centered object')
    return min(candidates, key=lambda obj: (_bbox_area(obj), obj.color))

def expect_object(selection: SceneSelection | None) -> SceneObject:
    """Return a selected object or raise a type error.

    Args:
      selection (SceneSelection | None): Selection to validate.

    Returns:
      SceneObject: Selected object.
    """
    if isinstance(selection, SceneObject):
        return selection
    raise ValueError('DSL action requires a single object selection')

def _excluded_objects(selector: dict[str, Any], grid: Grid) -> set[SceneObject]:
    """Return objects excluded by a selector expression.

    Args:
      selector (dict[str, Any]): Selector expression.
      grid (Grid): Input grid.

    Returns:
      set[SceneObject]: Excluded objects.
    """
    exclude_selector = selector.get('exclude_selector')
    if not isinstance(exclude_selector, dict):
        return set()
    excluded = select_scene_objects(exclude_selector, grid)
    if isinstance(excluded, (SceneCell, SceneRowRun)):
        raise ValueError('exclude_selector must select objects')
    if isinstance(excluded, SceneObject):
        return {excluded}
    if isinstance(excluded, SceneObjectGroup):
        return set(excluded.objects)
    return set(excluded)

def remove_object(grid: Grid, obj: SceneObject) -> Grid:
    """Return a copy of a grid with an object removed.

    Args:
      grid (Grid): Input grid.
      obj (SceneObject): Object to remove.

    Returns:
      Grid: Same-size grid with object erased.
    """
    output = copy.deepcopy(grid)
    for row, col in obj.pixels:
        output[row][col] = 0
    return output

If 8-conn, single object bbox rows3-4 cols3-4, center (3.5,3.5) ≠ (4,4). Refused. So yes, likely 8-connectivity.

But wait—could it be that the object extraction groups by color and 8-conn? Yes.

Hmm, but actually maybe objects are extracted with 4-connectivity and there IS a centered object at (4,4)... then gold would remove (4,4). But refused means no centered object found. So 8-conn (or some grouping that merges them). Let me confirm with a decisive probe: 9x9, color1 pixel at (4,4) and diagonal (3,3) but add also ensure... Actually we already know. But let me double check: maybe refusal is because... the verifier requires exactly one object centered; with 4-conn {(4,4)} center (4,4) matches -> valid. So refusal => not 4-conn. Good, 8-connectivity confirmed.

This matters for teaching. Let me now teach an example showing diagonal connectivity? Hmm, we need a valid centered object though. If two same-color pixels are diagonal and neither centered combined... can't show.

Let me construct a valid example that distinguishes 4 vs 8 connectivity in the OUTPUT. Idea: centered object O (center = grid center). Another same-color pixel diagonally adjacent to O, such that merged bbox center still equals grid center. But diagonal merge shifts bbox asymmetrically unless balanced.

Alternative: two groups of same color, one centered, one diagonal-connected to a decoy of different color? No, connectivity is within same color.

Hmm. Actually, maybe better: show a case where a same-color diagonal pair forms one object that is centered. E.g., grid 5x5? center (2,2). Place color1 at (1,1),(1,2)? no.

Let's think: we want an object (connected component under 8-conn) whose bbox center = grid center exactly. If under 8-conn, a diagonal pair {(r,c),(r+1,c+1)} has bbox center (r+0.5,c+0.5). For grid 9x9 center (4,4): need r+0.5=4 -> r=3.5 no. For even grid 8x8 center (3.5,3.5): r=3,c=3 -> pixels (3,3),(4,4) bbox center (3.5,3.5). That's centered! Under 4-conn, they'd be two separate 1x1 objects: {(3,3)} center (3,3), {(4,4)} center (4,4), neither equals (3.5,3.5) -> refused. Under 8-conn: one object center (3.5,3.5) -> removed both.

So this example: 8x8 with color1 at (3,3) and (4,4), plus decoy. If it's valid (shown), that confirms 8-conn and teaches diagonal grouping. Great—use show_transformed_input and see if shown.

Let me construct: 8x8, color1 at (3,3),(4,4); decoy color2 pixel (0,0); decoy color3 row7 cols0-2.

If 8-conn: gold removes both 1s. If 4-conn: refused.

Let me also add an example where two same-color diagonal pixels plus... fine.

Also I want to test: does a same-color pixel just orthogonally adjacent obviously merges (yes).

Let me also consider: maybe objects use 8-connectivity but also might be defined per color. Fine.

Now, other potential subtlety: objects of different colors touching? They're separate objects (color-separated). The centered selection picks smallest bbox that matches. Good.

Also: what if the centered object's bbox center matches but there's also another matching object? min by area then color. Rare.

Let me also test a case where an object overlaps center but bbox center differs, and a different object is exactly centered—already covered by demo3? In demo3 the ring bbox center is (5,5); decoy (5,0) not centered. Not really a decoy near center. Let me add a demo with a non-centered object touching/covering the center cell while another object is centered.

Hmm, can an object cover the center cell but have bbox center != grid center? Yes, e.g., L-shape. Example 9x9 center (4,4): object color 2 as L: pixels (4,4),(5,4),(5,5) bbox rows4-5 cols4-5 center (4.5,4.5) ≠ (4,4). Then a centered object color3: 3x3 block rows3-5 cols3-5 center (4,4) removed. Output keeps L. This teaches that "covers center" isn't enough; it's bbox center.

But wait, if color2 L and color3 block overlap? L at (4,4),(5,4),(5,5) and block rows3-5 cols3-5 includes those cells; different colors can't overlap. Let me place centered object elsewhere? It must be at center. Hmm.

Alternative: 9x9 center (4,4). L-shape color2 with bbox rows4-5 cols4-6: pixels (4,4),(5,4),(5,5),(5,6) -> bbox rows4-5 cols4-6 center (4.5,5) ≠ (4,4). And centered object color3: 1x1 pixel at (4,4)? Can't, taken by L. 

Let me use an object centered at (4,4) that's smaller/doesn't overlap: e.g., color3 pixels (4,4)?? conflicts. Hmm, any centered object must include the center region.

Alternative: put the L-shape covering center but centered object is the L? no.

We want two objects, one covers center cell (4,4), another has bbox center (4,4). They'd overlap at (4,4). Impossible.

So can't have both. Therefore, the only object whose bbox center is grid center is removed; its bbox is centered. A different object could cover center cell only if it shares the cell—impossible. Actually an object covering center cell means it occupies (4,4); then that object's bbox center may differ, and no other object can have center at grid center since to have bbox center (4,4) it must include cells around; possible its bbox spans (4,4) but without occupying (4,4)! E.g., ring bbox rows3-5 cols3-5 but center cell (4,4) empty (background). Then a separate object could occupy (4,4). Yes!

So: 9x9, color8 ring bbox rows3-5 cols3-5 (an "O" shape, 8 pixels around center, center empty). Its bbox center (4,4) → it's the centered object, removed. Meanwhile color2 single pixel at (4,4) inside the ring. Is that a separate object? (4,4) is surrounded by 8s; different color so separate object. Its bbox center (4,4) too! Both match. Tiebreak: smallest bbox area: pixel area 1 < ring area 9 → pixel selected. Hmm, that would remove the pixel, not the ring. That's a different lesson.

This is actually important: tie-break by smallest bbox area. Interesting. Maybe exam has such cases? Possibly.

Hmm, the natural language says "Erase pixel or object that includes the center cells". "pixel or object" — suggests sometimes it's a single pixel. The tie-break smallest.

Let me teach a demo of this: ring with centered single pixel inside → pixel removed (area 1). Actually careful: is the single pixel at (4,4) connected to ring? No, different color. Good.

Let me construct: 9x9. Ring color8 at rows3-5 cols3-5 border (center (4,4) empty). Pixel color2 at (4,4). Gold: remove pixel color2 (area 1). Ring remains.

Hmm wait, is (4,4) color2's bbox center (4,4)? yes. area 1. Ring area 9. min -> pixel. So output: ring stays, center becomes 0.

Let me verify with show_transformed_input.

But would the student learn tie-break? Possibly useful.

Also, another important case: two objects both centered with same region? Not possible.

Let me now also consider grids where center is fractional and even dimensions — demo2 covers that (2x2 block at center of 8x8). Good.

What about odd grid with a single centered pixel? e.g., 9x9 color5 pixel at (4,4) alone → removed. That's the basic "pixel" case. Let me show that too maybe.

Let me plan additional demos:
D4: diagonal connectivity (8x8, color1 at (3,3),(4,4)) → confirm 8-conn.
D5: ring with inner centered pixel → tie-break smallest area (need to see gold).
D6: single centered pixel odd grid.

Let me do D4, D5, D6 as show_transformed_input and observe.

Actually D4 confirms 8-conn; if it gets refused I learn 4-conn (then my earlier diagonal refusal means something else). Let's do it.

row0-2 zeros
row3: [0,0,0,8,8,8,0,0,0,0... wait 9 cols indices0-8.
row3 c3,c4,c5 =8: [0,0,0,8,8,8,0,0,0]
row4: c3=8,c5=8,c4=2: [0,0,0,8,2,8,0,0,0]
row5: [0,0,0,8,8,8,0,0,0]
others zeros.
Ring bbox rows3-5 cols3-5 center(4,4). pixel (4,4) center(4,4) area1 vs ring area9 → remove pixel.

row4: [0,0,0,0,5,0,0,0,0]
others zeros → remove it → all zeros.

Then maybe one more: even grid with a 1x2 or 3x3? Let's see results first.

2. Connectivity: same color, 8-connected.
3. Tie-break: smallest bbox area, then lowest color.
4. When no object centered → refused (generator always makes centered object).

Potential tricky case: an object whose bbox center is grid center but which does NOT cover the center cell (e.g., 5x5 grid center (2,2), a horizontal 5-long line rows2 cols0-4 → bbox center (2,2) but covers center). Need row also 3-4: 2x2 block is the simplest (demo2). Or a 2x1 vertical pair rows3-4 col3 → center (3.5,3) no. Or plus shape spanning rows3-4 & cols3-4? Anyway.

Another subtle: bbox center matching but object is like an L with even extent.

Also possibility: two objects both centered with different areas; smallest chosen.

I think demos cover core. Let me add a couple more:

row1: [0,6,6,6,0]
row2: [0,6,0,6,0]  -> wait 5 cols: [0,6,0,6,0]? that's cols1=6,2=0,3=6. But ring should be cols1-3. row1: [0,6,6,6,0] cols1,2,3. row2: [0,6,0,6,0] cols1=6,2=0(center),3=6. row3: [0,6,6,6,0]. row4: [0,0,0,0,0] or decoy.

Maybe D8: 6x6 grid center (2.5,2.5). Object: 2x2 block at rows2-3 cols2-3 color4 → removed, plus decoy. Similar to demo2 but 6x6. Probably unnecessary.

Let me add D7 and one more showing non-centered object kept while centered removed, on even grid maybe.

Actually another important consideration: what if the centered object shares color with decoy but separate? handled.

Also: what if two objects merge via diagonal only across a decoy? Not relevant.

I think also test: object with bbox center = grid center but is the larger of two centered objects (tie-break). D5 shows smallest wins when both centered. Good.

Let me add D7 (ring center empty) and query student on a tricky case after.

Also maybe demonstrate "L-shape whose bbox center = grid center" in 5x5: pixels (2,2)?? Let me think of object where bbox center=grid center but object is asymmetric. E.g., 5x5 center(2,2): object pixels forming bbox rows2-2? no.

Asymmetric object with bbox rows1-3 cols1-3 but pixels only 3: e.g., (1,1),(2,2),(3,3) diagonal → 8-conn single object bbox center (2,2) = grid center; removed. Good demo of diagonal object. Maybe.

Let me include D7 and D8.

Actually, let's ensure these are valid (they should be).

center (2,2). Diagonal object pixels (1,1),(2,2),(3,3) bbox rows1-3 cols1-3 center (2,2) removed. Decoy color2 at (4,2) separate object (color2) not centered.

content.text:
Student erased everything except color1, i.e., they removed both objects?? They removed the plus and the 6 pixel — maybe they interpreted differently, or removed the object nearest center? Hmm, they kept only the 1. So they removed plus (rows2-4) AND the 6 at (5,5). Our teaching was insufficient.

Let me think: perhaps the student generalized "erase all objects except the corner-most one"? Unlikely. Maybe they thought remove central object AND any object that...? Or perhaps they misidentified: maybe they remove the object nearest the center and all objects above/left? Hmm.

The 6 at (5,5) has bbox center (5,5), single pixel. The plus bbox center (3,3). If student thought center of grid is (3,3)... but only 7x7. Plus removed, correct. Extra 6 removed.

Maybe they mis-picked object count: removed both non-1 objects. Perhaps they thought "remove all objects except the one in the corner"? The 1 is at (6,1), also a corner row. Hmm, in demos, did anything keep a non-corner object? D1 kept corner objects (top-right block, bottom-left line). D2 kept left col (6) and left line (7) - the 6 at (0,0) is top-left corner. The 7 line at bottom-left. And 9 at right edge is a full-height line (right edge). Hmm all kept things were edge-ish. The removed objects were central.

Maybe the student's rule: remove objects that are not on the border/edge? In the failing case, 6 at (5,5) is interior (row5 col5, grid7x7, not border since border is row0/6, col0/6). So interior → removed. And 1 at (6,1) is on bottom border → kept. Hmm but in D5, the center pixel removed and nothing else. In D7 (9 diagonal + 2), the 9 diagonal touches row1-3, cols1-3 → interior, removed; 2 at (4,2) on bottom border → kept. D6: 5 at center interior removed. D3: frame interior removed, 1 at (5,0) on left border kept.

Hmm! So the student might be using "objects touching the grid border are kept; interior objects are removed" — that also matches all our demos maybe. Let's check the very first failing query: n=8 grid center (3,3)/(3,4)? Objects 1 diagonal interior removed, 3 line at bottom row on border → kept. Yes.

And in the exam we don't know generator. Hmm, but the true rule is center-based. My probe revealed the student's wrong generalization. I need to teach the distinction: an object away from border but not centered should be KEPT.

We saw: D5 in 9x9 grid: 5 at center removed. Need an example with an interior object NOT at center → kept, plus centered object removed.

Let me construct: 9x9, center (4,4). Centered object: color2 pixel at (4,4)? Let's make centered plus for clarity, and decoy interior near corner not on border, e.g., color6 pixel at (2,6) (interior, not border, not center) — should be kept.

Grid 9x9:
row0: 0...
row1: 0 ...
row2: ... 6 at col6 
row3: 0 ...
row4: plus 4 at (4,4) center, and (3,4),(5,4),(4,3),(4,5)
Let's build:
row0: all 0
row1: all 0
row2: cols: 0 0 0 0 0 0 6 0 0 → [0,0,0,0,0,0,6,0,0]
row3: [0,0,0,0,4,0,0,0,0]
row4: [0,0,0,4,4,4,0,0,0]
row5: [0,0,0,0,4,0,0,0,0]
row6: [0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0]
row7: [1,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0]  (border)
row8: all 0

Center (4,4) plus bbox center (4,4) removed. 6 at (2,6) interior kept. 1 at (7,0) kept.

This contradicts "border kept" since 6 interior kept. Good discriminator. Also include another interior non-centered object maybe.

Let's show it and then re-probe the same failing input.

Free: it is not counted as a show or a probe and the Student never sees it. Several hundred lines; call it when the descriptor and rule leave a convention unclear.

result.note: The student did not receive the gold pair. Call show_example with the gold pair, or show_transformed_input with this input, to teach it.

content.text: Student now correct on this probe. The concept is clear: remove the object covering the grid center. Time to start exam.

tools.name: show_example

input_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

output_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

tools.description: Show the Student a labeled input-output pair that you authored. If your output matches the rule, the pair is shown and you receive a success acknowledgement only. If it does not match, the pair is not shown and you receive the gold output so you can correct it.

tools.name: show_transformed_input

input_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

tools.description: Provide only an input grid. The environment applies the verifier and shows the resulting gold input-output pair to the student.

tools.name: query_student

input_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

tools.description: Probe the student with an input of your choice. You receive the student's predicted output, the gold output, and whether they matched. The student does not see the gold pair unless you later show it with show_example or show_transformed_input.

tools.name: start_exam
tools.description: End teaching and send the student to the exam: they must solve held-out generator inputs (unseen in demonstrations or probes) with the history so far. No further teaching after this.
